The Data Recipient agrees to process the Data only for the following purposes agreed with the HSCIC: 
Objective for processing:  
University of Leeds are requesting data to allow them to link HES records to those maintained by the Paediatric Intensive Care Audit Network (PICANet, http://www.picanet.org.uk/) which contains individual records of all patients admitted to intensive care in the UK and was established in 2002.
The project addresses three aims:
1) To assess long-term measures of outcome in children after admission to intensive care. The University of Leeds has already obtained information about mortality and now wants to explore further measures of outcome including the investigation of morbidity among such children such as future hospital stays. This information will be used to evaluate performance and improve service delivery by identifying where variation exists between units and diagnostic groups.
2) To better understand the pathways leading to admission to intensive care. At the same time the University is seeking information on hospital admissions and accident and emergency usage prior to PICU admission to enable it to possibly allow earlier identification of which children may require intensive care for resource planning.
3) To produce clinical decision aids to support decision making in paediatric intensive care settings including for children with life limiting conditions to identify whether a stay in paediatric intensive care is the most appropriate treatment option.
The purpose of this data linkage would be to support the national audit of paediatric intensive care services; enhance academic research in paediatric intensive care; and provide evidence to support clinical decisions about treatment options in paediatric intensive care for children with life-limiting conditions. These aims will provide an empirical evidence base for improving healthcare provision for children admitted to paediatric intensive care.
The University of Leeds will not release any record level data to third party organisations although University of Leeds will publish the results of their analysis in aggregate form with small numbers suppressed in line with the HES analysis guide.  No identifiable data will be released at any time.  
Processing activities:
The University of Leeds has requested data over a number of years because it is interested in events preceding admission and also to monitor the long term outcomes of children who are admitted to intensive care over an appropriate length of time. Data over a longer period of time will provide a valuable insight into the long term outcomes for these patients. The University of Leeds wants to look at how this has changed over time – mortality has reduced to under 4% and is no longer a reliable indicator of quality of care.  The University of Leeds needs the longitudinal data to evaluate underlying trends.
University of Leeds will supply identifiers and study ID for children resident in England in the PICANet database, University of Leeds would then require HSCIC to carry out data linkage to the HES data-sets and provide back the linked data-sets. No data will be linked for Northern Ireland.  
All data will be stored on a secure server at the University of Leeds.  No data will be released to third party organisations – all processing will be carried out on the secure server.

Specific outputs expected, including target date:

The intention is to publish results in high-quality peer-reviewed journals (such as The Lancet, Pediatrics, BMJ, Intensive Care Medicine, Paediatric Critical Care Medicine, Archives of Disease in Childhood) and to present them at relevant international and national conferences (such as European Society for Paediatric and Neonatal Intensive Care, Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, Paediatric Intensive Care Society, European Academy of Paediatrics, World Congress on Paediatric Critical Care, International Paediatric Palliative Care Conference). 
Findings will also be disseminated via the PICANet annual report which is publically available on the PICANet website, through paediatric clinical networks (such as the Paediatric Critical Care Clinical Commissioning Group, the Paediatric Intensive Care Society and the RCPCH) and to parents and carers via the PICANet families group, lay summaries produced on the PICANet website and through the press. 
The University of Leeds also holds an annual meeting to disseminate findings and discuss these findings with key stakeholders who include PICU clinicians, nurses and audit staff, commissioners, academic researchers, parent representatives, patient groups, funding bodies (such as HQIP and Scotland and Wales), other clinical audit representatives, and NHS England.  

Lay summaries of all of the research will be published on the PICANet website (previous research lay summaries are being reviewed by the PICU families group as will all future summaries to ensure they are accessible to the general reader).
Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care including target date:
At the end of the anticipated three year programme of work The University of Leeds hope to:     
1) Provide a more comprehensive assessment in peer-reviewed journals and annual assessment of morbidity following admission and subsequent discharge from paediatric intensive care which will allow the University to conduct more subtle comparisons of performance between different units.  In this way, The University may be able to identify best practice and quantify the healthcare needs of children post-discharge.  The University has been specifically asked to look at morbidity by the Department of Health (this is included in the University’s contract with HQIP as a specific item). The University has been criticised for not looking at longer-term morbidity in children in feedback from the DH via HQIP.  The University views HES data as the most efficient means of gaining long-term follow-up.
It is not practical or cost-effective to follow-up large numbers of children without using data linkage.
HES data has been used to assess post PICU discharge healthcare usage in the largest clinical trial ever conducted in paediatric intensive care (a randomized trial of hyperglycaemic control in pediatric intensive care. N Engl J Med 2014;370(2):107-18).  The University will attempt to assess health inequalities in the population in relation to their subsequent morbidity.  The University already knows that there are higher rates of admission to PICU from more deprived sections of the population and from the south Asian population.
The following NHS entities will benefit from this research by understanding how differences between services may modify the level of subsequent healthcare use: Paediatric Intensive Care clinicians and nurses, Specialist Commissioners for Paediatric Intensive Care, the Paediatric Critical Care Clinical Reference Group, NHS England Medical Directorate (particularly the National Clinical Director, Children, Young People and Transition to Adulthood and the NHS Medical Director for England).    Better models of care should result in reduced healthcare use and improved patient experience.’ 
2) Identify patient pathways leading to admission to intensive care and determine whether these vary between units. This will enable comparison between different models of service delivery. The University of Leeds will assess whether any variation affects subsequent outcome with a view to making recommendations on service improvement to NHS Trusts, CCG, Specialist Commissioners and via HQIP, the DH. The University of Leeds will assess whether there are health inequalities in accessing care and in the initial care pathway.  Recommendations on service improvement will be presented in reports to NHS England, Specialist Commissioners and NHS Trust CEOs and Clinical Directors. 
A more detailed examination of the care pathway leading to PICU admission will enable the University to recommend changes to local service provision (based on robust data) and to identify specific groups of patients who may require earlier intervention and support.  The University of Leeds would identify these groups in their reports on service improvement and in peer-reviewed publications.  So they will be identified in the literature for all of those identified as above.  The University of Leeds have strong links with commissioners, contributing data and analysis to a 10-year review of paediatric intensive care provision.  Ultimately it is commissioning that will facilitate change.  HQIP is also active in promoting change in local practice using local and national audit data and have a strong commitment to dissemination of national clinical audit outputs.  HQIP’s vision statement is ‘HQIP aims to improve health outcomes by enabling those who commission, deliver and receive healthcare to measure and improve our healthcare services.’ See http://www.hqip.org.uk/ as their whole website demonstrates their commitment to disseminating the findings of the audits they commission.  Their interest is solely in the audit component of our request.
The University of Leeds has already identified excess risk-adjusted mortality in South Asian children admitted to PICU and this is as yet unexplained. The data requested will give more information available on co-morbid conditions and the patient care pathways for south Asian children which will enable the University to identify differences that could explain their higher risk-adjusted mortality or, at least, eliminate these from the investigation.
3) Identifying whether the best place for children with life-limiting conditions to be treated is PICU will help those patients and their families to have better targeted care to improve their quality of life and ensure intensive care resources are targeted at the most appropriate population. The University of Leeds will submit the results to a peer-review journal, present these at conferences and also produce a final project report to the NIHR making the findings readily available to the clinical teams who are providing treatment.
This will very help a very specific target group of patients living with life-limiting conditions as well as their families and the clinical teams treating them by ensuring that they receive optimal care in the best environment.  All of these aims will provide information for healthcare providers that should enable them to improve services for patients.  This is a patient group that is increasing (see rising national prevalence of life-limiting conditions in children in England. Pediatrics 2012;129(4):e923 9). 
All of these aims will provide information for healthcare providers that should enable them to improve services for patients.
